Current [V12.4.1](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/blob/master/4.0/en/0x20-V12-Files-Resources.md#v124-file-storage):
>  Verify that files obtained from untrusted sources are stored outside the web root, with limited permissions.


"spin-off" issue from https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1065#issuecomment-944915831

I'm not too happy with this requirement. It feels a bit from old-style PHP crappy architecture, where file in public folder leads to RCE.

The main question is, should we just blindly disallow to store files in public folder in general, or make it a bit more flexible.

* sometimes files are expected to stay in public folder, like "public" images (or we ask them to serve from another domain? is it reasonable?)
* even if .php file is stored in public folder for "PHP application", it's important to avoid to execute it as PHP program code (by web-server configuration for example)

Basically it comes from a 3.0 requirement and I agree that the permissions/validation part is weird and that the webroot part is a little 90s but I still think the "web root" part is important and I don't want it to get lost.

I would propose the following, (note the updated CWE):

@elarlang @jmanico what do you think?

Well, not that easy.

> [MODIFIED] Verify that files obtained from untrusted sources are stored outside the web root so that there is no risk of accidental execution.

## Authorization

12.4 is file storage category and was removed from that perspective.

From file execution perspective, it should be 12.3 requirement.


## Client-Side execution

What about public content - like images, profile pictures, logos, some pdf files etc?

We have it kind of covered with othe requirement.

| # | Description | L1 | L2 | L3 | CWE |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **1.12.2** | [MODIFIED] Verify that user-uploaded files - if required to be displayed or downloaded from the application - are served by either octet stream downloads, or from an unrelated domain, such as a cloud file storage bucket. | | ✓ | ✓ | 646 |
| **12.5.2** | Verify that direct requests to uploaded files will never be executed as HTML/JavaScript content. | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | 434 |

I have made proposal to merge them: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1406

It would be wasting resources to serve static images via program code and may actually cause good DoS vectors.

But those are more client-side oriented.


## Server-Side execution

Now the question to solve is - why it may happen, that users can upload as "public content" something, which is executed on the server side via HTTP request as program code.

I would call it business logic problem.

| # | Description | L1 | L2 | L3 | CWE |

For example, backup files (e.g. .bak), temporary working files (e.g. .swp), compressed files (.zip, .tar.gz, etc.) and other extensions commonly used by editors should be blocked unless required. | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | 552 |

What we clearly don't have is (in whatever wording): Verify that files obtained from untrusted sources are not executed as program code when directly accessed with HTTP request.

I re-read this and do agree that in the context of uploading files, we need to stage uploaded files in directories that are permissioned properly. This is a fundamental requirement to secure file upload.

I vote we revive 12.4.1 with a requirement like:

_Verify that uploaded files from untrusted sources are being stored in a secure, non-web-accessible directory or other data store, with restrictive file system permissions to prevent unauthorized access or execution._

> Verify that files obtained from untrusted sources are not executed as program code when directly accessed with HTTP request.

It does not take into account public static files by their logical meaning, such as profile images,

I think the problem to address (written in https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1087#issuecomment-1568391839) is:

> What we clearly don't have is (in whatever wording): Verify that files obtained from untrusted sources are not executed as program code when directly accessed with HTTP request.

Good point. How about:

_Verify that uploaded files from untrusted sources are being stored in a secure, non-web-accessible directory or other data store, with restrictive file system permissions to prevent unauthorized access or execution. **If files like profile images must be stored in a public directory, ensure they are not executable or contain malware.**_

>  If files like profile images must be stored in a public directory, ensure they are not executable

"executable" here is not that clear I guess, you can execute file if you have such permissions. My guess is that the original requirement comes from PHP era - there files are "executed" with direct HTTP request, I'm not sure that execute permissions are required for this or file-read permissions for a web server (like Apahce) is enough?

>  ... or contain malware.

This is covered by 12.4.2: _Verify that files obtained from untrusted sources are scanned by antivirus scanners to prevent upload and serving of known malicious content._

Profile images are generally safe if you deploy them in a read only directory. The problems of the past were that an image might be a gif, but it’s really a shell script can be executed if it’s delivered with executable file permission. Actually directory needs executable permissions to diverse the directory. It’s just the file itself that only needs to be read only.

I still think it’s sensible if you’re uploading an image that you want to be in a public web directory there’s no reason for the file to be anything other than read only.  The problem specifically with gif’s have been relatively recent within the last couple of years.

How about:

_Verify that uploaded files from untrusted sources are being stored in a secure, non-web-accessible directory or other data store, with restrictive file system permissions to prevent unauthorized access or execution. **_If files like profile images must be stored in a public directory, ensure the files permissions are read only._**_
@elarlang to provide an updated option

I re-read it, and I think it is not clear, what is the problem to solve with this proposed requirement?

So the re-usable template for everyone to be used in every issue:
"To prevent /attack, vulnerability/ Verify that / what need to be done to solve or avoid the problem /"

It’s to prevent any uploaded code from being executed on the server, typically a form of command injection via malformed images and other uploaded files that can be executed as code. There is a rich history of this form of attack.

If malformed image is executed, it can be 2 reason:
* problem in image processing library (known vuln, not up to date library) or the way it is called (command injection)
* image itself is being executed as program code, e. g. so called polyglots (we have requirement 14.3.6 to limit the file extensions being allowed)

So, as concluded before, the only "problem to solve" is that "Verify that files uploaded or generated by untrusted input stored in public folder are not executed as program code when accessed directly with HTTP request".

The problem with the image library (which has dozens of historical examples) should be handled in requirement to keep components updated.

> image itself is being executed as program code, e. g. so called polyglots (we have requirement 14.3.6 to limit the file extensions being allowed)

The whole point of file permission limitations is that this class of attack allowed even files with .gif extensions (or in the distant past wmf files and other file types), and with magic bytes claiming to be gif to still be executable ik certain cases. This is why you want to set the file permissions of uploaded files that you publically deploy to be read only. It’s a very basic and easy to implement control that fully shuts this category of attacks down.

Gifs, ICO, SVG and others have had this problem.

Or let me ask another question. Would you want an uploaded file of any type that you stage up in a public directory to be permissioned as executable? This seems like a very bad idea to me.
What and why is going to execute it?

Why? Why do attackers attack? I don’t understand the question. 

There is a *lot* of research on uploaded images being executable historically. For a wide variety of reasons depending on the web server type, the app server type, and the image type.

So are you suggesting that staging up uploaded files in a public directory with file permissions being set to executable to be an acceptable practice? Really?

Kind of "here we go again" with demagogy.

If you allow user to upload (edit: a php) file to public folder that is executed when directly accessed with an HTTP request, it does not require to have "executable" permissions. Read-only is enough.

And if it comes to "executable", then something - some process must execute it. This was my question, what process and why it can execute the file?

Since its in a public directly any user can navigate to that file. JS files can impact node servers. Gif-Jar’s impact Java servers. There are numberous situations again depending on the server type.

Setting piblically available uploaded files to be read only (depending on the server and other factors) shuts down:

- Remote Code Execution (RCE)
- Web shell attacks
- File inclusion vulnerabilities (LFI/RFI)
- Privilege escalation
- Denial of Service (DoS) through malicious scripts
- Soe forms of Cross-site scripting (XSS) and other injection-based attacks

And even if other ASVS items (like file validation) address these issues, setting uploaded publically staged files to read only - is a fairly standard secure coding practice.

Have had this discussion here before:
* executable may mislead to `+x` permission, but this is not the key or reason here

* if to remove the "public folder" part, it requires different access or attack vector and I consider this to not be in the scope for the requirement.


> Verify that files uploaded or generated by untrusted input which are stored in a public folder are not executed as server-side program code when accessed directly with an HTTP request.
I hear you. All good. Public it is.

I'm still concerned about this. And Elar you have other things to do and I am ok if you ignore this. But here is one last attempt at an argument here.

There are several other scenarios where an uploaded file can be unexpectedly executed, depending on the environment, platform, and misconfigurations. Modern platforms can execute files more dynamically.

A. Files Executed via Web Server Behavior
	•	Misconfigured servers (Apache, Nginx, IIS) might treat uploaded files as scripts based on:
	•	File extension (e.g., .php, .jsp, .aspx)
	•	MIME type sniffing
	•	Script handler mappings (e.g., Apache’s AddHandler)
	•	Path traversal bugs can allow attackers to upload to locations outside of intended directories (e.g., /var/www/html/admin/)

B. Files Placed in Executable Paths
	•	If uploaded files end up in a path that is:
	•	Scanned by the runtime or container, such as:
	•	Python’s PYTHONPATH
	•	Java’s classpath
	•	Node’s require() resolution directories
	•	Served from a script-enabled directory, such as a .php file in /uploads with AllowOverride All

C. Files Triggered by Extensions or Applications
	•	Image upload with embedded script (e.g., polyglot file: valid image + PHP code)
	•	Office documents with macros (e.g., .docm, .xlsm)
	•	Executable installers, .exe, .msi, .app, when opened on user systems
	•	Shell scripts that get run by automation systems (e.g., uploaded .sh picked up by CI/CD)

D. Archive Uploads That Get Extracted
	•	ZIP or TAR files uploaded, then extracted server-side without sanitization, can:
	•	Place files in sensitive locations (../ traversal in zip)
	•	Inject executable code into other files (e.g., override .bashrc)
	•	Exploit symlinks in the archive

E. File Parsing Libraries with RCE or DoS Vulnerabilities
	•	ImageMagick (“ImageTragick”), ExifTool, FFmpeg, etc., have had critical RCE bugs triggered during parsing of malicious files.

F. Uploaded Files Interpreted by External Services
	•	PDFs or images uploaded to a server might be sent to third-party OCR/analysis APIs, where parsing could be exploited
	•	Serverless functions that process uploaded files may have poor sandboxing

G. Content Embedding in Trusted Contexts
	•	Uploaded SVG files embedded inline in HTML can run inline JavaScript
	•	Uploaded files reused in email templates, user profile pages, etc., may enable stored XSS or template injection

So I'd suggest:

_Verify that uploaded files are not executed, interpreted, or otherwise processed as code by the application, server, or any downstream system, regardless of upload location. This includes scenarios involving direct URL access, inclusion in server-side processing pipelines, or automatic extraction and handling._

TLDR: if you see any uncovered areas that is not covered in the ASVS, it does not make the current requirement invalid.

Scope and context is something to take into account and keep in mind.

---

> A. Files Executed via Web Server Behavior
> • Misconfigured servers (Apache, Nginx, IIS) might treat uploaded files as scripts based on:
> • File extension (e.g., .php, .jsp, .aspx)
> • Script handler mappings (e.g., Apache’s AddHandler)

Those are covered by the requirement 5.3.1

> • MIME type sniffing

MIME sniffing is a browser side action, covered by 3.4.4. If there could be server-side mime-sniffing and program code execution because of that, it is covered by 5.3.1.

> • Path traversal bugs can allow attackers to upload to locations outside of intended directories (e.g., /var/www/html/admin/)

Path traversal is a separate underlining problem, covered by 5.3.2.

---

> B. Files Placed in Executable Paths
> • If uploaded files end up in a path that is:
> • Scanned by the runtime or container, such as:
> • Python’s PYTHONPATH
> • Java’s classpath
> • Node’s require() resolution directories

There is a need for other problem in the program code to be able to load the file, most likely covered by 5.3.2

> • Served from a script-enabled directory, such as a .php file in /uploads with AllowOverride All

I would say it is covered by 5.3.1.

---

> C. Files Triggered by Extensions or Applications
> • Image upload with embedded script (e.g., polyglot file: valid image + PHP code)

It is covered by 5.3.1

> • Office documents with macros (e.g., .docm, .xlsm)

Not sure what precise impact is meant here. From the issue point of view, it is covered by 5.3.1.

> • Executable installers, .exe, .msi, .app, when opened on user systems

Out of scope, or covered by 5.1.1 + 5.4.3


> • Shell scripts that get run by automation systems (e.g., uploaded .sh picked up by CI/CD)

It is a separate problem. Not sure we have it directly addressed.

---

> D. Archive Uploads That Get Extracted
> • ZIP or TAR files uploaded, then extracted server-side without sanitization, can:

Covered by 5.2.2

> • Place files in sensitive locations (../ traversal in zip)

Covered by 5.3.3

> • Inject executable code into other files (e.g., override .bashrc)

Requires already writing or code injection as a precondition.

> • Exploit symlinks in the archive

Covered by 5.2.5


---

> E. File Parsing Libraries with RCE or DoS Vulnerabilities
> • ImageMagick (“ImageTragick”), ExifTool, FFmpeg, etc., have had critical RCE bugs triggered during parsing of malicious files.

Requires vulnerability in a library that processing a file, covered by 15.2.1

---

> F. Uploaded Files Interpreted by External Services
> • PDFs or images uploaded to a server might be sent to third-party OCR/analysis APIs, where parsing could be exploited
> • Serverless functions that process uploaded files may have poor sandboxing

What happens in external service, is out of scope.

---

> G. Content Embedding in Trusted Contexts
> • Uploaded SVG files embedded inline in HTML can run inline JavaScript

First, the issue is about server-side program code execution.

For described situation, SVG must be sanitized, covered by 1.3.4

> • Uploaded files reused in email templates, user profile pages, etc., may enable stored XSS or template injection

This is area of safe generation of output document and you can not fix it with limiting uploaded files. Quite far away from file upload and executing as a program code.

The recommendation
> Verify that uploaded files are not executed, interpreted, or otherwise processed as code by the application, server, or any downstream system, regardless of upload location. This includes scenarios involving direct URL access, inclusion in server-side processing pipelines, or automatic extraction and handling.

There are different execution vectors here - one is by an HTTP request and another from so-called server side execution.

So the requirement 5.3.1 focuses on the first one, and you focus on the second one. The likelihood for the first one is for sure higher than likelihood for the second one.

But I feel like it requires some other vulnerabilities as precondition to happen, otherwise we create a requirement that "Verify that user-uploaded files are not executed as program code by backend processes" - but why it should happen?

With all these other ways uploaded files can we executed, and as we see there are many, I still think "public folder" sends the wrong message. It's way too specific, IMO. I think that surgically removing "public folder" we still capture the essence of what you want to see without being overly narrow.
And I am unfairly looping with you Elar and I'm sorry. We just have a different opinion here and it's ok to let it go.

To address the 5.3.1 - it requires fix in a web server configuration. It is one precise problem to address and it should not contain anything else. If there is some other vulnerabilities to address, it should be done separately.

The problem(s) you address require other solutions or vectors. But what we can not have as a requirement is "Do not have RCE". We need to address every underlying problem separately.

We have also requirement to say, that application must not be able to change it's own code:
> 13.4.3	Verify that application code or functionality can only be changed via the standard update or build process and not directly in production through application functionality or some other direct modification mechanism.

So can you name me scenarios, where user-controlled code is executed as program code, without any other underlying problems (like LFI, path traversal).

1) Dynamic code exection:

const userInput = getUserFile();  
eval(userInput);

2) Template injection:

template = "{{ " + userInput + " }}"
rendered = jinja2.Template(template).render()

3) Deserialization:

ObjectInputStream in = new ObjectInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(userInputBytes));
Object obj = in.readObject(); 

4) REPL or Interactive Console Exposure

Serverless Function Runtimes / Plugin Syste
(User submits code as part of a plugin or extension and it is executed in a runtime sandbox)

5) Code generation features:

User submits code as part of a plugin or extension and it is executed in a runtime sandbox

6) CI/CD and Build Pipeline Execution

7) WebAssembly or Lua/JS Plugins

8) "eval-as-configuration” Pattern

9) ML/AI Model Evaluation APIs

I have more if you want me to keep going.

I feel like my previous comment was ignored, to highlight some points:

> But what we can not have as a requirement is "Do not have RCE". **We need to address every underlying problem separately**.

> So can you name me scenarios, where user-controlled code is executed as program code, **without any other underlying problems** (like LFI, path traversal).

RCE is an impact, not the cause.

To take the parallel from the client-side field, we can not say "do not have XSS", but we need to address every underlying problem separately.

I get the point of "RCE is an impact, not the cause". I see where you are coming from. It's a fair point.

But let me try again from a different perspective.

In traditional web hosting (Apache, Nginx static file serving, PHP apps, etc.), the "public folder" was the root directory exposed directly to the browser, everything in it was world-readable, and anything outside of it was considered application or server logic and protected by the web server.

Modern frameworks like Next.js, Spring, Laravel, Django, Ruby on Rails and others still often include a public or static directory, **_but the usage has changed:_**

**1. Static assets are explicitly handled**
- Frameworks bundle and compile assets during build time.
- Static files go to a public/ or static/ folder (e.g. images, CSS, JS).
- These files are served via CDN or web server as raw files.

**2. App logic is not exposed publicly**

- App routes are compiled into server-side code or API routes.
- Files and routes are protected by the runtime (e.g., Node.js server, serverless function handlers).
- Files are often inside a /pages, /routes, or /src folder—not directly exposed to the public.

**3. Deployment platforms further abstract "public"**
Vercel, Netlify, AWS Lambda, and others:
- Build the app and deploy only needed static files to an edge/CDN.
- Dynamically generate server-side content from handlers.
- Make "public" a conceptual boundary, not necessarily a filesystem one.

This is why I don't like the term "public folder" - modern frameworks and deployment pipelines use this idea more logically than literally now, with dynamic content rendered securely and separated from public exposure. And that makes file upload dangers a lot different than the PHP days of public folder.

So because of how significantly the concept of a public folder has changed in modern frameworks since the PHP days of old, I'd like to see...

| # | Description | L1 | L2 | L3 | CWE |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---:| :---: | :---: |
5.3.1 | Verify that files uploaded or generated by untrusted input are not executed as server-side program code. | 1 | v5.0.be-12.4.1
-- | -- | -- | --

...to make sure that the changes in how modern frameworks handle files today are considered. 

**_The way that it stands today is really only specific to one type of framework and is not at all universal to all web apps._**

> Verify that files uploaded or generated by untrusted input are not executed as server-side program code.

This is vague and not realistically testable, this is exactly "do not have RCE" requirement, it is not actionable. You may think one scenario for this in your head, but technically it covers LFI, RFI, outdated library or whatever reason how to reach there.

If you want to cover the topic further, then the first sign of quality should be that you don't mix n+1 topics into it (external CDN, CSS files, etc).

The requirement 5.3.1 is to address configuration problem. If you want to address an architecture problem, it does not make this requirement wrong. There _may_ be need for a separate requirement.

But I have said and tried to explain it so many times here, those explanations are ignored and I can not see point to continue it like that.

Hi @jmanico, if I understand correctly, Elar would prefer that the current requirement stays with the current focus which I think makes sense given the context of the section. He also noted above how other requirements handle some of your other concerns but noted that maybe an additional requirement could be needed.

I also note that we have strayed slightly from the original topic Jim so if it is ok with you, I would prefer to close this issue and ask you to open a separate issue if you have unanswered questions or would like to see an additional requirement following [this comment above](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1087#issuecomment-2781523958).
